Leeuwarden
lay'oo-var-den
n. (capital of Friesland, Dutch Leeuwarden, Frisian Ljouwert; seat of the Frisian stadholders and of the provincial Reformed church)
Dutch Leeuwarden, from Old Frisian Lintwerd or Leeuwerd, a werd or dwelling-mound by the Linde water; the lion in the modern spelling is a later folk reading.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Leeuwarden is the chief city of Friesland, built on three dwelling-mounds above the marsh and made the seat of government by the Saxon and then the Habsburg lords of the province. Its Reformation was slow, bloody and divided. The first executions for the gospel in Friesland were carried out there in the 1530s, and among those put to death at Leeuwarden in 1531 was Sicke Freerks, beheaded for a second baptism; it was that execution, in the town where he afterwards lived, which first shook the priest Menno Simons out of his place and set him on the road to the Anabaptist leadership. The city held for Spain until 1580, when the province went over to the Republic, the Mass was forbidden, and the Reformed church was established. From that year Leeuwarden was the seat of the Frisian synod, the residence of the stadholders of the Frisian branch of the house of Nassau, and the administrative centre from which the Reformed ministry of a province full of Mennonites was organised and paid. The dictionary keeps it as the plainest Frisian instance of a hard truth: that the ground on which a Reformed church was finally planted had usually been watered first by blood shed over a doctrine that church did not hold.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town, incorporated with certain privileges; a province as a country belonging to a kingdom or state; and a mound as an artificial elevation of earth.

expand to see more

CITY, n. [L. civitas.] A large town; in a more appropriate sense, a corporate town; a town or collective body of inhabitants, incorporated and governed by particular officers.

PROVINCE, n. [L. provincia.] A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; a region of country; a division of a kingdom.

MOUND, n. Something raised as a defense; an artificial elevation of earth; a bank; a bulwark.

MARSH, n. A tract of low land, usually or occasionally covered with water, or very wet and miry; a swamp; a fen.

MARTYR, n. [Gr. a witness.] One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith, or in defense of any belief.

Key Scripture

Rev 6:9 — "And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:"

Mat 5:10 — "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Act 8:1 — "And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles."

Psa 126:5 — "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy."

Modern Corruption

Frisian capital where the first executions for the gospel were carried out in the 1530s, and which became the seat of the provincial Reformed synod after 1580.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest difficulty is the mixed inheritance. Leeuwarden's first martyrs died as Anabaptists, for a doctrine of baptism the later established church of the city rejected; and that established church, once it had the magistrate behind it, was not always gentle with the Mennonites who remained. The dictionary does not smooth this over. It holds believer's baptism with the 1689 Confession and therefore stands nearer those first sufferers than the Frisian synod did; and it holds that the use of the sword against a man's conscience in matters of religion was wrong when Charles the Fifth's officers did it and wrong when a Reformed magistracy did it.

The principle to recover is that the roll of the slain is kept by God and not by the party. “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) does not say that every soul under that altar had every doctrine right. It says why they were killed. A town's church history is read truly only when the dead of the other party are counted in it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek martus (G3144), a witness, hence a martyr; Hebrew dimah (H1832), tears.

expand to see more

Greek psuche (G5590) — a soul, a life; “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay, to butcher; Revelation 6:9.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; “they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake”, Matthew 5:10.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad, as seed; “they were all scattered abroad”, Acts 8:1.

Hebrew dimah (H1832) — tears, weeping; “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy”, Psalm 126:5.

Usage

"“the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — the first Frisian executions for the gospel, Leeuwarden in the 1530s."

"“And at that time there was a great persecution against the church” (Act 8:1) — the beheading of Sicke Freerks in 1531."

"“They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5) — seat of the Frisian synod from 1580."
